result.topic_en: Using mean values of the lunar and solar hourly motions and of the node, Euler computes the coefficient (m+n+2k)/(n-m) and gives a table of corrections for the Moon's true longitude in its orbit at mid-eclipse, then estimates the error caused by deviations of true from mean motions.

§ 27. Ex hac ergo tabula satis exacte locus lunae in sua orbita ad medium cujusque eclipsis momentum assignari poterit, etiamsi motus horarius verus diversus sit a medio. Quanquam enim verus motus horarius lunae a medio fere 5', et verus motus horarius solis a medio 5'' discrepare potest, tamen inde in coëfficientem $\frac{n+m+2k}{n-m}$ non adeo magnum discrimen redundat. Augeamus namque, ut discrimen fiat maximum, valorem litterae $n$, 300'', at valorem litterae $m$ minuamus 5'' ita ut numerator augmentum capiat 295'' et denominator 305'', eritque $\frac{n+m+2k}{n-m} = \frac{2435}{2134} = 1,14105$[?], cujus valoris defectus a praecedente medio est $= 0,02931 = \frac{1}{34}$. items.quote: Hi valores, quia a veris nunquam adeo notabiliter discrepant, sufficiunt ad formulam, quam supra (§ 13) eruimus, ad longitudinem lunae in orbita medio eclipsis inveniendam.
items.english: These values, since they never differ very notably from the true ones, suffice for the formula derived above (§ 13) for finding the Moon's longitude in its orbit at the middle of an eclipse.

items.quote: Ex hac ergo tabula satis exacte locus lunae in sua orbita ad medium cujusque eclipsis momentum assignari poterit, etiamsi motus horarius verus diversus sit a medio.
items.english: From this table the Moon's place in its orbit at the middle moment of any eclipse can be assigned fairly exactly, even if the true hourly motion differs from the mean.
